passage: A screening group in the Kowalski laboratory identified a compound that suppresses alcohol dehydrogenase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several acetaldehyde concentrations, with and without 40 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to acetaldehyde, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

options.A: The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
options.B: The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
options.C: The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases
options.D: The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases

questions.explanation: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/5, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor.
questions.trap: Expecting inhibition to shrink at high substrate; the inhibited velocity is one fifth of control at every [S], so substrate does not overcome it.

questions.stem: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?

options.A: Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
options.B: Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
options.C: Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax
options.D: Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate

questions.explanation: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site.
questions.trap: Choosing the option in which Km rises with inhibitor, the signature of competitive inhibition, the opposite of what is being confirmed.

questions.stem: If the uninhibited Vmax is 100 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
questions.explanation: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 100/5 = 20 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows.
questions.trap: Choosing 16.7 µmol/min, which is 100/6, by adding 1 to the factor of 5 instead of dividing the uninhibited Vmax by 5.

questions.stem: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?

options.A: The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
options.C: The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
options.D: Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis

questions.explanation: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km).
questions.topic: Enzyme inhibition: trap on Km vs Vmax
questions.trap: Believing noncompetitive inhibitors raise Km because they lower velocity, when Km is unchanged and only Vmax falls.

questions.stem: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?

options.A: Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
options.B: Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
options.C: Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site
options.D: Substrate-level competition by a structural analog

questions.explanation: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways.
questions.trap: Choosing substrate-analog competition, which the passage rules out by noting the compound has no structural resemblance to acetaldehyde.
